question.problem:
The entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & k & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]$
equals $2.$ Find the value of $k.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & k & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}k & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}|-0|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-k-6)-0+1(6-k) \\  & =-k-6+6-k \\  & =-2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{12} & =(-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-2-2) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{21}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2k}\cdot 4 \\  & =-\frac{2}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{21}^{′}=2$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{k} & =2 \\ -2 & =2k \\ -\frac{2}{2} & =k \\ k & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$
